title: Cerebral cavernous hemangioma: dilated capillaries with thin septa
vignette: A 30-year-old man with a history of epilepsy comes to the office for follow-up. He has a history of recurrent seizures that start as jerky, rhythmic movements of his left leg and gradually spread to involve the entire left side of his body. The patient frequently loses consciousness and has been witnessed to have a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Neuroimaging has revealed a focal lesion in the right motor area. He has been treated with several antiepilepsy drugs, but his seizures have remained poorly controlled. Surgery is performed to remove the lesion, and the excised brain tissue shows a 1.5-cm mass composed of engorged purplish clusters. Microscopy shows numerous dilated capillaries with an endothelial lining separated by a thin layer of fibrous connective tissue. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

clues.text: seizures that start as jerky, rhythmic movements of his left leg and gradually spread
clues.note: A focal seizure with 'Jacksonian march' (spread along the motor homunculus) points to a structural lesion in the contralateral motor cortex.

clues.text: a 1.5-cm mass composed of engorged purplish clusters
clues.note: A well-circumscribed 'mulberry-like' cluster of engorged purple vascular spaces is the gross appearance of a cavernous hemangioma.

clues.text: numerous dilated capillaries with an endothelial lining separated by a thin layer of fibrous connective tissue
clues.note: Dilated, thin-walled vascular channels (endothelium-lined) separated by scant fibrous septa - lacking normal intervening brain/elastic/smooth muscle - is the histology of a cavernous hemangioma.

whatMatters: A well-circumscribed 'mulberry-like' cluster of dilated, thin-walled capillaries lined by endothelium and separated by thin fibrous septa (no normal brain in between) = CAVERNOUS HEMANGIOMA (a vascular malformation). Its poor structural support makes it prone to bleed and irritate cortex, causing seizures. Answer A.
strategy: Read the histology: abnormal DILATED capillaries/blood vessels with thin adventitia lacking elastic fibers and smooth muscle = cavernous hemangioma. Reject the tumors and aneurysm: ependymoma (perivascular pseudorosettes), glioblastoma (pseudopalisading necrosis + tumor cells), Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8, spindle cells), and saccular (berry) aneurysm (a focal arterial outpouching from myointimal hyperplasia, at the circle of Willis).

eliminations.label: Ependymoma - perivascular pseudorosettes (your pick)
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a CNS tumor (4th ventricle in children, spinal cord in adults) whose cells form perivascular PSEUDOROSETTES. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: the lesion here is a cluster of dilated blood vessels (a malformation), not a cellular tumor with pseudorosettes. ✅ Correct if: a tumor with perivascular pseudorosettes.

eliminations.label: Glioblastoma - pseudopalisading necrosis
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an aggressive astrocytoma with areas of necrosis surrounded by tumor cells (pseudopalisading) and microvascular proliferation. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: histology shows dilated vessels with thin septa, not a necrotic glial tumor. ✅ Correct if: pseudopalisading necrosis with malignant glial cells.

eliminations.label: Kaposi sarcoma - HHV-8 spindle cells
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: an HHV-8-driven vascular tumor with elongated SPINDLE cells (skin/GI/respiratory in immunosuppressed patients). ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it shows spindle-cell proliferation, not simple dilated capillaries with thin septa, and is not a typical solitary brain mass. ✅ Correct if: violaceous skin nodules in HIV with spindle cells.

eliminations.label: Saccular (berry) aneurysm - arterial outpouching
eliminations.detail: WHAT IT IS: a focal outpouching of a cerebral artery (thickened intima/myointimal hyperplasia, stretched adventitia) at the circle of Willis. ❌ WHY IT FAILS: it is a single arterial dilation prone to subarachnoid hemorrhage, not a cluster of dilated capillaries causing focal seizures. ✅ Correct if: a berry aneurysm (subarachnoid hemorrhage risk).

reasoning: A well-circumscribed cluster of engorged purple vascular spaces causing focal seizures
Histology: dilated, thin-walled capillaries lined by endothelium, separated by thin fibrous septa (no normal brain between)
This is a cavernous hemangioma - a low-flow vascular malformation prone to bleed and irritate cortex
mechanism: Cavernous hemangiomas (cavernous malformations) are benign VASCULAR MALFORMATIONS that can involve deep tissues including the liver and brain. Grossly they appear as well-circumscribed 'MULBERRY-LIKE' clusters of engorged purple vascular channels. Histologically they consist of abnormally DILATED, thin-walled capillaries/sinusoidal blood vessels lined by a single endothelial layer and separated only by scant FIBROUS connective-tissue septa, with a thin adventitia that LACKS elastic fibers and smooth muscle and NO intervening normal brain parenchyma. This reduced structural support gives them a tendency to LEAK/bleed (often with hemosiderin deposits) and to irritate surrounding cortex. In the brain, they are frequently asymptomatic but can cause SEIZURES (as here, a focal motor seizure with Jacksonian spread from a right motor-cortex lesion) or focal neurologic deficits; surgical resection is indicated for intractable epilepsy or progressive deficits. The distractors are distinguished histologically: ependymoma (perivascular pseudorosettes), glioblastoma (pseudopalisading necrosis), Kaposi sarcoma (HHV-8 spindle cells), and saccular aneurysm (an arterial outpouching from myointimal hyperplasia).

difficulty.label: 🧠 Knowledge
difficulty.text: First Aid Path/Neuro > cavernous hemangioma: vascular malformation; dilated thin-walled vessels with thin fibrous septa (no elastic/smooth muscle, no normal brain between); 'mulberry' gross; bleeds; seizures.

difficulty.label: 📖 Comprehension
difficulty.text: Dilated capillaries with thin septa (no normal brain) = cavernous hemangioma (malformation), not a tumor.

difficulty.label: 🔤 Vocab
difficulty.text: Unsure on cavernous hemangioma/malformation, vascular malformation, Jacksonian march, pseudorosette, or pseudopalisading necrosis? Tell me which.

difficulty.label: 🨤 Distractor
difficulty.text: Ependymoma (pseudorosettes), glioblastoma (pseudopalisading necrosis), Kaposi (spindle cells), berry aneurysm (arterial outpouching) have different histology.

difficulty.label: 🗒️ Other
difficulty.text: Bank: cavernous hemangioma = dilated thin-walled vessels + thin fibrous septa (no normal brain); prone to bleed; causes seizures.

keywords.front: Dilated thin-walled vessels with thin fibrous septa, no normal brain between

keywords.back: 'Mulberry-like' cluster of engorged purple vascular spaces
Thin walls lacking smooth muscle/elastic support -> leak + cortical irritation
Arterial outpouching (myointimal hyperplasia) at circle of Willis

firstAid.detail: Path: dilated thin-walled vessels + thin fibrous septa; mulberry gross; bleeds/seizures.
Path > ependymoma (pseudorosettes), GBM (pseudopalisading), Kaposi (spindle), berry aneurysm.
Neuro > seizures/hemorrhage; resect if intractable epilepsy/deficits.

memoryHook: A brain 'mulberry' of floppy dilated capillaries with only thin fibrous walls (no muscle, no brain between) = cavernous hemangioma - it oozes blood and sparks seizures.
